```{r}
#| label: library

options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
library(housepi)
housepi_theme_set()
set.seed(42)
```

Let's briefly recall the concept of Bayesian data augmentation for the case of epidemiological outbreaks.

Bayesian data augmentation is a computational strategy that expands the parameter space by introducing augmented variables (also referred to as hidden or latent variables) to facilitate sampling from the posterior.

For example, consider a single infectious individual $i$.
Imagine that someone reported the date of symptom onset $T^\mathrm{ons}_{i}$.
We can think of the observation process that returned that value as some function of the actual real time of onset, $t^\mathrm{ons}_{i}$.

We can introduce latent infection times $t_{i}$, defined as the difference between the onset time and the augmented incubation period $\tau^\mathrm{inc}_{i}$, so that 
$$t^\mathrm{ons}_{i} = t_{i} + \tau^\mathrm{inc}_{i},$$
where the incubation period is distributed according to a prior.

Say $x$ the data of a single household (onset date and status), $z$ its augmented variables (infection time and incubation period) and $\theta$ the vector of parameters.
The joint posterior then reads
$$p(\theta, z \mid x) \varpropto
  \underbrace{p^\mathrm{obs}(x \mid \theta, z)\, p^\mathrm{transm}(x \mid \theta, z)}_{\text{likelihood}}\;
  \underbrace{p^\mathrm{augm}(z \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}_{\text{prior}},$$
where the likelihood is the transmission term $p^\mathrm{transm}$ times the observation term $p^\mathrm{obs}$ (the latter only when an observation node is defined, so it contracts to transmission otherwise), and the prior is the augmented-variable prior $p^\mathrm{augm}$ times the parameter prior $p(\theta)$.

We here explain how to associate individual augmented variables in housepi for minimal examples.

# Build augmented variables

Similarly to parameters, augmented variables require definitions for models and proposals needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo.
In many applications, augmented variable definitions can also depend on the dataset or on model parameters to be inferred.

# Link arguments to source

We can declare the source of any argument value according to the convention using the \@ symbol
$$
\mathrm{argument@source}
$$
which reads "argument at source".
E.g. "visit_day\@D" will source the value from individual data "visit_day", "beta\@P" from the current value for the parameter "beta", etc.


<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
<div>

| Source     | Symbol | Examples          |
|------------|:------:|:-----------------:|
| Augmented  | A      | infection_time    |
| Data       | D      | visit_day\@D      |
| Group Rate | G      | susceptibility\@G |
| Numeric    | N      | 14                |
| Parameter  | P      | beta\@P           |

</div>
</div>

Notice that a variable name without explicit source will automatically be assumed to be an augmented variable^[However sometimes it could be necessary to disambiguate, which can be done with the source \@A.].
Similarly, there's no need to specify the source of a numeric value.

More in general, definition arguments `value`, `min` and `max` can be linked to external values in the following ways

# Status specific definitions

In many applications, the same augmented variable has to be augmented according to different rules depending on the individual.
This is the case for example of infection times for symptomatic and asymptomatic members.
We can address this issue in housepi using status specific definitions, as opposed to generic definitions valid for all positive status individuals.
Let's consider the case of a survey that reported symptoms within a follow-up period and tested every household member only when a first individual showed symptoms and after 10 days.
Let's use `status = 1` to tag symptomatic individuals and `status = 2` to tag asymptomatic.
We decide to augment infection times of symptomatic members as shown in [Get Started](housepi.html), i.e. informed by reported onset date.
For asymptomatic members we draw the infection time uniformly within the period of the follow-up.

```{r}
#| label: status-specific-augmented
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)

onset_tommy <- 5
hhmodel <- data.frame(id = c("tommy", "gina"),
                      house_id = "house_1",
                      start_date = onset_tommy,
                      study_period = 10,
                      status = c(1, 2),
                      onset_date = c(onset_tommy, NA)) |>
  new_housepi_model("case_ascertained") |>
  add_parameter(alpha = 0.001, beta = 0.07, gamma = 0.9, size_ref = 4) |>

  # associate augmented definitions
  add_augmented(
    # augmented infection time for symptomatic members
    # here we use a generic definition
    infec_time = onset_date@D - incub_period,
    incub_period = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1),

    # augmented infection time for asymptomatic members
    # here we use a status specific definition, with priority over generic
    infec_time = list(status = 2, prior = "uniform",
                      loc = start_date@D, max = study_period@D)
  )
```

We could run the inference and extract the results as usual.
However, sometimes it is useful to check if augmented variable draws evolve as expected.
We can do so by providing the `id` of individuals whose augmented variables we want to store through the argument `id_draws` of `run_inference()`.

```{r}
#| label: augmented-infection-time-plot
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Density plots of augmented infection times for two household members.
# run inference following traces of specific individuals
hhmodel |>
  # store augmented draws of "tommy" and "gina"
  run_inference(id_draws = c("tommy", "gina")) |>
  get_augmented_draws() |>
  posterior::subset_draws(variable = "infec_time$", regex = TRUE) |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_dens(facet_args = list(ncol = 1)) +
  geom_vline(data = data.frame(xintercept = onset_tommy),
             aes(xintercept = xintercept), linetype = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = onset_tommy + c(-10, 10))
```

We see that since we assumed the infection of the asymptomatic member to happen after the onset of the index, the model logically makes it more probable to occur closer to that limit.

# Example: estimate incubation period distribution

For simplicity, we start testing data augmentation on a dataset which is not a household survey.
Instead we consider a simulated report documenting the days when a number of cases were exposed to infection and the days of symptom onset.

```{r}
#| label: generate-delays-data
# use an example script for generate delays
source("helpers/generate_delays.R")
# generate delays according to a gamma distribution
true_mean <- 2.2
true_var <- 1.4
dataset <- generate_delays_report(223, mean = true_mean, var = true_var,
                                  report_error = 0.73)
head(dataset)
```
Note that here the data has no demographic structure: we are implicitly assuming that all individuals live in distinct households.

Assuming the incubation period to be described by a gamma distribution, we want to estimate its `mean` and `var` by augmenting the infection and onset times.
Following the decomposition introduced above, the incubation period enters the *augmented prior* $p^\mathrm{augm}(z \mid \theta)$, while the reported onset day enters the *observation* term $p^\mathrm{obs}(x \mid \theta, z)$.

We rely on the "test" model, which carries no transmission dynamics ($p^\mathrm{transm} = 1$), and build the whole augmentation from definitions:

- the infection time `.infec_time` is drawn uniformly within the reported exposure window;
- the incubation period `incub_period` is the quantity we model, gamma distributed with the inferred `mean` and `var` and bounded to a plausible range;
- the onset time `.onset_time` follows deterministically as their sum.

Finally, an observation node ties the latent onset time to the data: we model the reported onset day `onset_mid` as a noisy measurement of the true onset time, normally distributed around `.onset_time`.

```{r}
#| label: incubation-example-setup
# generate an instance of the household model class
hhmodel <- dataset |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # reported onset mid-point: noisy measurement of the reported interval
    onset_mid = 0.5 * (onset_min + onset_max + 1.)
  ) |>
  new_housepi_model("test") |>
  # define the gamma distribution parameters to be inferred
  add_parameter(
    mean = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0.1, max = 5, proposal = "normal"),
    var = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0.1, max = 5, proposal = "normal")
  ) |>
  # augmented variable definitions
  add_augmented(
    # infection time uniform within the reported exposure window
    # min = 0 by default for uniform; + 0.99 spans the whole reported day
    .infec_time = list(prior = "uniform", max = exposure_max@D + 0.99,
                       proposal = "normal"),
    # incubation period gamma by mean/variance, bounded to a plausible range
    incub_period = list(prior = "gamma", mean = mean@P, var = var@P,
                        min = 0.1, max = 14, proposal = "normal"),
    # onset time follows deterministically as their sum
    .onset_time = .infec_time + incub_period
  ) |>
  # observation model for the observed mid-point
  add_observation("onset_mid", obs = "normal", mean = .onset_time, sd = 0.3)
```

```{r}
#| label: inference-traces
#| fig-height: 3
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for mean and variance parameters with three parallel chains.
#|  Overlaying orange lines indicate the values used for the simulation.
results <- hhmodel |>
  # store augmented draws of "7" and "13"
  run_inference(id_draws = c("7", "13"))

# plot traces of parameter draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_parameter_draws(results)) +
  geom_hline(data = data.frame(parameter = c("mean", "var"),
                               simulated = c(true_mean, true_var)),
             aes(yintercept = simulated))
```

```{r}
#| label: augmented-draws-traces
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for individual augmented variables across three MCMC chains.
#|  Incubation period for two subjects (IDs 7 and 13).
# plot traces of augmented draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_augmented_draws(results))
```

In this example we had to introduce auxiliary augmented variables `.onset_time` and `.infec_time`.
The prefix `.` we added to the names is a convention to ensure that housepi will not store the associated draws.

# More about models and proposals

```{r}
#| label: color-scheme-augmented
#| include: false
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "orange")
```

When it comes to data augmentation, we might need to explore different options for the Monte Carlo moves.
In the following examples we show the differences between move choices that can be performed.
As shown in [Priors and proposals](priors_and_proposals.html), we can do the testing with the "test" model.
We always recommend a visual assessment before choosing a new move.

```{r}
#| label: augmented-sample-model
#| warning: false

# with model (default sample)
results <- new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_augmented("sample_model", prior = "normal", mean = 14) |>
  run_inference()
```

```{r}
#| label: trace-augmented-sample
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plot of a single augmented variable sampled from the model.
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_augmented_draws(results))
```

```{r}
#| label: trace-log-likelihood
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plot of the pointwise per-household log-likelihood.
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_log_lik_draws(results))
```
